+WINDOWS XP/Win2K/98 VISUAL C++ 6.0 AND 7.0 COMPILATION
+
+  The Visual C++ distribution targeted at Windows XP, Win2K, or Windows
+  98 does not provide any stock workspace (DSW) or project files (DSP)
+  except for those included with third party libraries. Instead, there
+  is a `configure' program that must be built and run that creates build
+  environments to satisfy various requirements.
+
+  The Visual C++ system provides three different types of "runtimes" that
+  must match across all application, library, and DLL code that is built. The
+  `configure' program creates a set of build files that are consistent for
+  a specific runtime selection.
+
+  The three options for runtime support are:
+
+    1) Dynamic Multi-threaded DLL runtimes (VisualDynamicMT).
+    2) Static Single-threaded runtimes (VisualStaticST).
+    3) Static Multi-threaded runtimes (VisualStaticMT).
+    4) Static Multi-threaded DLL runtimes (VisualStaticMTDLL).
+
+  In addition to these runtimes, the VisualMagick build environment allows
+  you to select whether to include the X11 libraries in the build or not.
+  X11 DLLs and headers are provided with the VisualMagick build environment.
+  Most Windows users do not use X11 so they will prefer to build without
+  X11 support.  Without X11 support, the `animate', `display', and `import'
+  will not work.
+
+  This leads to five different possible build options, which should cover
+  almost any particular situation.  The default binary distribution is built
+  using #1 from above with the X11 libraries included.  This results in an
+  X11 compatible build using all DLL's for everything and multi-threaded
+  support (the only option for DLL's).
+
+  To do a build for your requirements, simply go to the configure subdirectory
+  under VisualMagick and open the configure.dsw workspace (for Visual C++
+  6.0) or configure.sln (for Visual C++ 7.0). Set the build configuration to
+  "Release" under the
+
+      "Build..., Set Active Configuration..."
+
+  menu.
+
+  Build and execute the configure program and follow the on-screen
+  instructions.  Generally you can accept the configuration defaults.
+
+  The configure program provides a button titled
+
+     Edit "magick_config.h"
+
+  Clicking this button allows you to edit `magick_config.h' in a Windows
+  Notepad window for optionally changing any preprocessor defines.
+  This file is copied to `magick\magick_config.h'.  You may safely open
+  `magick\magick_config.h', modify it, and recompile without re-running the
+  configure program.  In fact, using the notepad program to edit the copied
+  file may be preferable since it preserves the original `magick_config.hi'
+  file.
+
+  Key user tunables in magick_config.h include:
+
+    MAGICKCORE_QUANTUM_DEPTH (default 16)
+
+      Specify the size of PixelPacket color Quantums (8, 16, or 32).
+      If you need to preserve the fidelity of 16-bit images (gray, png,
+      etc), use 16.  If you want to work in remote sensing or if you are
+      a mad scientist you might consider 32.  Note, that a quantum-depth
+      16 uses 4-times as much memory as the default quantum-depth of 8,
+      whereas a quantum-depth of 32 uses 16-times as much memory.
+
+    MAGICKCORE_INSTALLED_SUPPORT (default undefined)
+
+      Define to build an ImageMagick which uses registry settings or embedded
+      paths to locate installed components (coder modules and configuration
+      files).  The default is to look for all files in the same directory
+      as the executable.
+
+    ProvideDllMain (default defined)
+
+      Define to include a DllMain() function ensures that the ImageMagick
+      DLL is properly initialized without participation from dependent
+      applications.  This avoids the requirement to invoke IntializeMagick()
+      from dependent applications but only works for DLL builds.
+
+  After creating your build environment you can proceed to open the DSW
+  (or SLN) file that was generated in the VisualMagick directory and build
+  everything from there.
+
+  In the final DSW file you will find a project call "All". In order to
+  build everything in the distribution, select this project and make it the
+  "active" project. Set the build configuration to the desired one (Debug,
+  or Release) and do a "clean" followed by a "build".  You should do the
+  build in a specific way:
+
+    1) Make the "All" project the active project (Bold)
+       Right click on the All project and select "Set As Active Project"
+    2) Select "Build..., Clean" 3) Select "Build..., Build" 4) Go get some
+    coffee unless you have a very fast machine!.
+
+  The "Clean" step is needed in order to make sure that all of the target
+  support libraries are updated with any patches needed to get them to
+  compile properly under Visual C++.
+
+  All of the required files that are needed to run any of the command
+  line tools will be found in the "bin" subdirectory of the VisualMagick
+  subdirectory.  This includes EXE, and DLL files. You should be able to test
+  the build directly from this directory without having to move anything to any
+  of the global SYSTEM or SYSTEM32 areas in the operating system installation.
+
+  Note #1:
+
+  The Visual C++ distribution of ImageMagick comes with the Magick++
+  C++ wrapper by default.  This add-on layer has a large number of demo
+  and test files that can be found in ImageMagick\Magick++\demo, and
+  ImageMagick\Magick++\tests. There are also a variety of tests that use
+  the straight C API as well in ImageMagick\tests.
+
+  All of these programs are NOT configured to be built in the default
+  workspace created by the configure program.  You can build these demos
+  and test programs to be built by checking the box in configure that says:
+
+    "Include all demo and test programs"
+
+  In addition, there is another related checkbox (checked by default) that
+  causes all generated project files to be created standalone so that they
+  can be copied to other areas of you system.
+
+  This is the checkbox:
+
+    "Generate all utility projects with full paths rather then relative paths"
+
+  Visual C++ uses a concept of "dependencies" that tell it what other
+  components need to be build when a particular project is being build.
+  This mechanism is also used to ensure that components link properly.
+  With this feature enabled, you should be able to nab a copy of...
+
+    VisualMagick\utilities\UTIL_convert_xxx_exe.dsp  (for C)
+
+  or
+
+    VisualMagick\Magick++\demo\UTIL_demo_xxx_exe.dsp (for C++)
+
+  and pop it into the notepad program, modify it (carefully) to your needs
+  and be on your way to happy compiling and linking.
+
+  You can feel free to pick any of the standard utilities, tests, or demo
+  programs as the basis for a new program by copying the project and the
+  source and hacking away.
+
+  The choice of what to use as a starting point is very easy.
+
+  For straight C API command line applications use something from:
+
+    ImageMagick\tests or ImageMagick\utilities (source code)
+    ImageMagick\VisualMagick\tests or ImageMagick\Visualmagick\utilities (project - DSP)
+
+  For C++ and Magick++ command line applications use something from:
+
+    ImageMagick\Magick++\tests or ImageMagick\Magick++\demo (source code)
+    ImageMagick\VisualMagick\Magick++\tests or ImageMagick\VisualMagick\Magick++\demo (project - DSP)
+
+  For C++ and Magick++ and MFC windows applications use:
+
+    ImageMagick\contrib\win32\MFC\NtMagick (source code)
+    ImageMagick\VisualMagick\contrib\win32\MFC\NtMagick (project - DSP)
+
+  Note #2:
+
+  The ImageMagick distribution is very modular. The default configuration
+  is there to get you rolling, but you need to make some serious choices
+  when you wish to change things around.
+
+  The default options are all targeted at having all the components in one
+  place (e.g. the "bin" directory of the VisualMagick build tree). These
+  components may be copied to another folder (such as to another computer).
+
+  The folder containing the executables and DLLs should contain all the
+  configuration files, *.xml.
+
+  The "bin" folder should contains all EXE's and DLL's as well as the very
+  important "coder.xml" file.
+
+  With this default setup, you can use any of the command line tools and run
+  scripts as normal.  You can actually get by quite nicely this way by doing
+  something like "pushd e:\xxx\yyy\bin" in any scripts you write to execute
+  "out of" this directory.
+
+  By default the core of ImageMagick on Win32 always looks in the place were
+  the exe program is run from in order to find all of the files as well as
+  the DLL's it needs.
+
+
+ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES
+
+  You can use the "System" control panel to allow you to add and delete what
+  is in any of the environment variables. You can even have user specific
+  environment variables if you wish.
+
+  PATH
+
+    This sets the default list of places were Windows looks for EXE's
+    and DLL's.  Windows CMD shell seems to look in the "current" directory
+    first - no matter what, which may make it unnecessary to update the PATH.
+    If you wish to run any of utilities from another location, you must
+    add the path to your "bin" directory in. For instance, you might add:
+
+       D:\CVS\ImageMagick\VisualMagick\bin
+
+    to do this for the default build environment like I do.
+
+  MAGICK_HOME
+
+    If all you do is modify the PATH variable, the first problem you will run
+    into is that ImageMagick may not be able to find any of its "modules".
+    Modules are all the IM_MOD*.DLL files you see in the distribution.
+    There is one of these for each and every file format that ImageMagick
+    supports. This environment variable tells the system were to look for
+    these DLL's.  The compiled in "default" is "execution path" - which says
+    - look in the same place that the application is running "in".  If you
+    are running from somewhere other then "bin" - this will no longer work
+    and you must use this variable.  If you elect to leave the modules in
+    the same place as the EXE's (a good idea), you can simply set this to
+    the same place as you did the PATH variable. In my case:
+
+       D:\\ImageMagick\coders
+
+    This is also the place were ImageMagick expects to find the configuration
+    files, *.xml, including module.xml, type.xml, etc.
+
+    One cool thing about the modules build of ImageMagick is that you can
+    now leave out file formats and lighten you load.  If all you ever need is
+    GIF and JPEG, simply drop all the other DLL's into the local trash
+    can and get on with your life.  However, always keep the "xc" format,
+    since ImageMagick uses it for internal purposes.
+
+  Also. You can elect to changes these things the good old "hard-coded"
+  way. Two #defines are applicable.
+
+  defines.h has
+
+      #define MagickConfigurePath  "c:\\ImageMagick\\"
+
+  To view any image in a Microsoft window, type
+
+      convert image.ext win:
+
+  Make sure Ghostscript is installed, otherwise, you will be unable to
+  convert or view a Postscript document, and Postscript standard fonts will
+  not be available.
+
+  You may use any standard web browser (e.g. Internet Explorer) to browse
+  the ImageMagick documentation.
+
+  The Win2K executables will work under Windows 98.
+

+
+                             Installing Magick++
+
+General
+
+In order to compile Magick++ you must have access to a standard C++
+implementation. The author uses  gcc 3.1 (GNU C++) which is available under
+UNIX and under the Cygwin UNIX-emulation environment for Windows. Standards
+compliant commercial C++ compilers should also work fine. Most modern C++
+compilers for Microsoft Windows or the Mac should work (project files are
+provided for Microsoft Visual C++ 6.0).
+
+It was decided that Magick++ will be around for the long-haul, so its API
+definition depends on valuable C++ features which should be common in all
+current and future C++ compilers. The compiler must support the following
+C++ standard features:
+
+   * templates
+   * static constructors
+   * C++-style casts (e.g. static_cast)
+   * bool type
+   * string class (<string>)
+   * exceptions (<exception>)
+   * namespaces
+   * Standard Template Library (STL) (e.g. <list>, <vector>)
+
+The author has personally verified that Magick++ compiles and runs using the
+following compiler/platform combinations:
+
+                            Tested Configurations
+
+       Operating System         Architecture             Compiler
+ SunOS 5.6, 5.7, 5.8
+ ("Solaris 2.6, 7, & 8)      SPARC             GCC 3.0.4
+ SunOS 5.7 ("Solaris 7")     SPARC             Sun Workshop 5.0 C++
+
+ SunOS 5.8 ("Solaris 8")     SPARC             Sun WorkShop 6 update 2 C++
+                                               5.3
+ FreeBSD 4.0                 Intel Pentium II  GCC 2.95
+
+ Windows NT 4.0 SP6a         Intel Pentium II  Visual C++ 6.0 Standard
+                                               Edition
+
+ Windows XP                  Intel Pentium IV  Visual C++ 6.0 Standard
+                                               Edition Service Pack 5
+ Windows '98 + Cygwin 1.3.10 Intel Pentium III GCC 2.95.3-5
+ Windows NT 4.0 SP6a         Intel Pentium II  GCC 2.95.3-5
+ Windows XP + Cygwin 1.3.10  Intel Pentium IV  GCC 2.95.3-5
+
+Users of Magick++ have reported that the following configurations work with
+Magick++:
+
+                      Other Known Working Configurations
+
+ Operating

+ Linux 6.0                           <Alexander.Zimmermann@fmi.uni-passau.de>

+Please let me know if you have successfully built and executed Magick++
+using a different configuration so that I can add to the table of verified
+configurations.
+
+  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+                                 Unix/Linux
+
+Building From Source
+
+Magick++ is now built using the ImageMagick configure script and Makefiles.
+Please follow the installation instructions provided by its README.txt file.
+The following instructions pertain to the Magick++ specific configuration
+and build options.
+
+To install ImageMagick plus Magick++ under Unix, installation should be
+similar to
+
+./configure [ --prefix=/prefix ]
+make
+make install
+
+The library is currently named similar to 'libMagick++.a' (and/or
+libMagick++.so.5.0.39) and is installed under prefix/lib while the headers
+are installed with Magick++.h being installed in prefix/include and the
+remaining headers in prefix/include/Magick++.
+
+To influence the options the configure script chooses, you may specify
+'make' option variables when running the configure script. For example, the
+command
+
+
+     ./configure CXX=CC CXXFLAGS=-O2 LIBS=-lposix
+
+specifies additional options to the configure script.  The following table
+shows the available options.
+
+             Environment Variables That Effect Configure
+
+     Make Option
+      Variable                         Description
+
+         CXX         Name of C++ compiler (e.g. 'CC -Xa') to use
+                     compiler 'CC -Xa'
+      CXXFLAGS       Compiler flags (e.g. '-g -O2') to compile with
+
+      CPPFLAGS       Include paths (-I/somedir) to look for header
+                     files
+                     Library paths (-L/somedir) to look for
+                     libraries. Systems that support the notion of a
+       LDFLAGS       library run-path may additionally require
+                     -R/somedir or '-rpath /somedir' in order to
+                     find shared libraries at run time.
+        LIBS         Extra libraries (-lsomelib) required to link
+
+Installing Linux RPMs
+
+Dr. Alexander Zimmermann maintains Linux RPMs of ImageMagick and Magick++.
+These may be downloaded from
+ftp://ftp.forwiss.uni-passau.de/pub/linux/local/ImageMagick/. This site is
+mirrored periodically to the ImageMagick linux directory and from there to
+the many ImageMagick and Linux mirror sites. Please note that the default
+version of the C++ compiler delivered with the system may not be sufficient
+to support Magick++. Use of GCC 2.95 or later is strongly recommended under
+Linux.
+  ------------------------------------------------------------------------
+
+                       Windows '9X, NT, 2000, ME, & XP
+
+Visual C++
+
+Windows '95 through Windows XP are supported by the ImageMagick source
+package for NT available in the 'win2k' subdirectory of the ImageMagick ftp
+site (and mirrors).  The ImageMagick source package for NT provides sources
+to ImageMagick, Magick++, add-on libraries (e.g. JPEG), and a ready-made
+Visual C++ 6.0 build environment. Please read the configuration and build
+instructions in README.txt (under the heading "Windows Win2K/95 VISUAL C++
+6.0 COMPILATION") in order to build Magick++.
+
+Cygwin & GCC
+
+It is possible to build both ImageMagick and Magick++ under the Cygwin
+Unix-emulation environment for Windows NT. Obtain and install Cgywin from
+http://www.cygwin.com/ .   An X11R6 environment for Cygwin is available
+from  http://www.cygwin.com/xfree/ .To build using Cygwin and GCC, follow
+the instructions for building under Unix. ImageMagick and Magick++ do not
+yet include support for building Windows DLLs under Cygwin so do not enable
+dynamic libraries when building ImageMagick.

+This file records noteworthy changes in Magick++.
+
+(5.5.2)
+  * Added adaptiveThreshold() method.
+  * Added colorMapSize() method.
+  * Added DrawablePushClipPath, DrawablePopClipPath, and DrawableClipPath.
+
+(5.5.1)
+  * Fixed a Color memory allocation problem which became evident when
+    using the Magick++ DLL.
+  * Completed implementation of Image textEncoding() method.  Oops!
+
+(5.4.9)
+  * Added the Image textEncoding() method and an encoding option to
+    DrawableText to support specifying "UTF-8" (Unicode) text encoding.
+  * Added the Image compare() method to support comparing two similar
+    images and obtaining error values.
+  * Magick++ compiles as a DLL under Visual C++ 7.0.
+
+(5.4.8)
+  * The image type() method now also specifies the output image type
+    to use while writing.
+  * Added a profile() method to Image to support adding, removing,
+    and retrieving named embedded application profiles.
+  * Magick++ compiles as a DLL under Visual C++ 6.0.
+
+(5.4.7)
+  * No changes to report.
+
+(5.4.6)
+  * Magick++ library no longer depends on C++ iostreams APIs.
+  * Added DrawableTextUnderColor class to set text underbox color.
+
+(5.4.5)
+  * Drawable classes have been re-written to use ImageMagick's draw.h
+    APIs.
+  * Fixed a nasty bug when reporting some forms of errors.  The bug
+    was causing an exception in error.c.
+  * Template API implementation cleanup.
+  * Rationalized some parameter types.
+  * New method, Pixels::getConst() to obtain read-only pixels.
+  * DrawableDashArray() prefers an array of type 'double' rather than
+    'unsigned int'.  Please use the new form.
+  * Composite images are output as embedded inlined Base64 when
+    preparing MVG data.
+  * Blob class supports encoding and decoding Base64 data.
+  * New method, Image::ping to ping a Blob.
+
+(5.4.4)
+  * Fixed a bug in DrawableDashArray.
+  * Numerous consistency improvements based on findings from Gimpel lint.
+  * Added endian method to Image, and endianImage class to STL.h in

+    the notion (e.g. TIFF).
+  * DrawableCompositeImage was not working.  Now it does.
+

+
+This is Magick++, the object-oriented C++ API to the ImageMagick
+image-processing library, the most comprehensive open-source image
+processing solution available. Read the release notes for Magick++.
+
+Magick++ supports an object model which is inspired by PerlMagick.
+Magick++ executes faster than PerlMagick since it is accessed from a
+compiled language rather than from a scripting language. This makes it more
+suitable for Web CGI programs which must start-up and execute quickly.
+Images support implicit reference counting so that copy constructors and
+assignment incur almost no cost. The cost of actually copying an image (if
+necessary) is done just before modification and this copy is managed
+automatically by Magick++. De-referenced copies are automatically deleted.
+The image objects support value (rather than pointer)  semantics so it is
+trivial to support multiple generations of an image in memory at one time.
+
+Magick++ provides integrated support for the Standard Template Library (STL)
+so that the powerful containers available (e.g. deque, vector, list, and
+map)  can be used to write programs similar to those possible with PERL &
+PerlMagick. STL-compatable template versions of ImageMagick's list-style
+operations are provided so that operations may be performed on multiple
+images stored in STL containers.
+
+Documentation
+
+Detailed documentation are provided for all Magick++ classes, class methods,
+and template functions which comprise the API.
+
+Obtaining Magick++
+
+Magick++ is included as part of ImageMagick source releases and may be
+retrieved via ftp or Subversion.
+
+Installation
+
+Once you have the sources available, follow these detailed installation
+instructions for UNIX and Windows.
+
+Usage
+
+A helper script named Magick++-config is installed under Unix which assists
+with recalling compilation options required to compile and link programs
+which use Magick++.  For example, the following command will compile and
+link the source file example.cpp to produce the executable example (notice
+that quotes are backward quotes):
+
+     c++ `Magick++-config --cxxflags --cppflags --ldflags --libs` \
+       -o example example.cpp
+
+Windows users may get started by manually editing a project file for one of
+the Magick++ demo programs.
+
+Reporting Bugs
+
+Please report any bugs via the Magick++ Bug Tracking System at
+http://www.imagemagick.org/discourse-server/.
+
+Related Packages
+
+Users who are interested in displaying their images at video game rates on a
+wide number of platforms and graphic environments (e.g. Windows, X11, BeOS,
+and Linux/CGI) may want to try PtcMagick, which provides a simple interface
+between Magick++ and OpenPTC.

+#!/bin/sh
+#
+# Configure options script for re-calling Magick+ compilation options
+# required to use the Magick++ library.
+#
+#
+
+prefix=@prefix@
+exec_prefix=@exec_prefix@
+libdir=@libdir@
+includedir=@includedir@
+
+usage='Usage: Magick++-config [--cppflags] [--cxxflags] [--exec-prefix] [--ldflags] [--libs] [--prefix] [--version]
+
+ For example, "magick.cpp" may be compiled to produce "magick" as follows:
+
+  "c++ -o magick magick.cpp `Magick++-config --cppflags --cxxflags --ldflags --libs`"'
+
+if test $# -eq 0; then
+      echo "${usage}" 1>&2
+      exit 1
+fi
+
+while test $# -gt 0; do
+  case "$1" in
+    -*=*) optarg=`echo "$1" | sed 's/[-_a-zA-Z0-9]*=//'` ;;
+    *) optarg= ;;
+  esac
+  case $1 in
+    --prefix=*)
+      prefix=$optarg
+      ;;
+    --prefix)
+      echo $prefix
+      ;;
+    --exec-prefix=*)
+      exec_prefix=$optarg
+      ;;
+    --exec-prefix)
+      echo $exec_prefix
+      ;;
+    --version)
+      echo '@PACKAGE_VERSION@ Q@QUANTUM_DEPTH@ @MAGICK_HDRI@'
+      ;;
+    --cflags)
+      echo "-I${includedir} @MAGICK_PCFLAGS@"
+      ;;
+    --cxxflags)
+      echo '@MAGICK_CXXFLAGS@'
+      ;;
+    --cppflags)
+      echo '@MAGICK_CPPFLAGS@'
+      ;;
+    --ldflags)
+      echo '@MAGICK_LDFLAGS@'
+      ;;
+    --libs)
+      echo "-L${libdir} -lMagick++ -lMagickWand @MAGICK_LIBS@"
+      ;;
+    *)
+      echo "${usage}" 1>&2
+      exit 1
+      ;;
+  esac
+  shift
+done
+

+#
+# Makefile for Magick++ demo programs
+#
+# Copyright Bob Friesenhahn, 1999, 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003
+#
+AUTOMAKE_OPTIONS = 1.8 foreign nostdinc
+
+AM_CPPFLAGS = -I$(top_builddir) -I$(top_srcdir)/Magick++/lib -I$(top_srcdir)
+
+check_PROGRAMS = analyze button demo detrans flip gravity piddle shapes zoom
+
+LDADD = ../lib/libMagick++.la
+
+analyze_SOURCES = analyze.cpp
+button_SOURCES  = button.cpp
+demo_SOURCES    = demo.cpp
+detrans_SOURCES = detrans.cpp
+flip_SOURCES    = flip.cpp
+gravity_SOURCES = gravity.cpp
+piddle_SOURCES  = piddle.cpp
+shapes_SOURCES  = shapes.cpp
+zoom_SOURCES	= zoom.cpp
+
+EXTRA_DIST = model.miff smile.miff smile_anim.miff tile.miff
+
+CLEANFILES = *_out.* ir.out # SunWS_cache
+
+ZOOM_FILTERS = bessel blackman box catrom cubic gaussian hamming hanning hermite \
+ lanczos mitchell point quadratic sample scale sinc triangle
+ZOOM_GEOMETRY = 600x600
+
+if WIN32_NATIVE_BUILD
+SRCDIR='$(shell @WinPathScript@ $(srcdir)/)'
+else
+SRCDIR='$(srcdir)/'
+endif
+
+MAGICK_ENV = $(SHELL) $(top_builddir)/magick.sh
+
+# FIXME: MinGW needs Windows path form of srcdir here (or pass as command argument)
+check:
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./analyze '$(srcdir)/model.miff'
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./button
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./demo
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./flip
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./gravity
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./piddle
+	@$(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./shapes
+	for filter in $(ZOOM_FILTERS) ; do  \
+	  echo "$$filter ..." ; \
+	  $(MAGICK_ENV) SRCDIR=$(SRCDIR) $(MEMCHECK) ./zoom -filter $$filter -geometry $(ZOOM_GEOMETRY) '$(srcdir)/model.miff' zoom_$${filter}_out.miff ; \
+	done
+

+Summary of MVG Primitives and Syntax
+====================================
+
+MVG ignores all white-space between commands. This allows
+multiple MVG commands per line. It is common convention to
+terminate each MVG command with a new line to make MVG easier
+to edit and read. This syntax description uses indentation in
+MVG sequences to aid with understanding. Indentation is
+supported but is not required.
+
+Metafile wrapper syntax (to support stand-alone MVG files)
+----------------------------------------------------------
+
+  push graphic-context
+   viewbox 0 0 width height
+    [ any other MVG commands ]
+  pop graphic-context
+
+
+Pattern syntax (saving and restoring context)
+---------------------------------------------
+
+  push pattern id x,y width,height
+   push graphic-context
+    [ drawing commands ]
+   pop graphic-context
+  pop pattern
+
+an example is (%s is a identifier string)
+
+  push defs
+   push pattern %s 10,10 20,20
+    push graphic-context
+     fill red
+     rectangle 5,5 15,15
+    pop graphic-context
+    push graphic-context
+     fill green
+     rectangle 10,10 20,20
+    pop graphic-context
+   pop pattern
+  pop defs
+
+For image tiling use
+
+  push pattern id x,y width,height
+   image Copy ...
+  pop pattern
+
+Note you can use the pattern for either the fill or stroke like
+
+  stroke url(#%s)
+
+    or
+
+  fill url(#%s)
+
+Clip-path syntax
+----------------
+
+ The clip path defines a clipping area, where only the contained
+ area will be drawn upon.  Areas outside of the clipping area are
+ masked.
+
+  push defs
+   push clip-path %s
+    push graphic-context
+     rectangle 10,10 20,20
+    pop graphic-context
+   pop clip-path
+  pop defs
+  clip-path url(#%s)
+
+Individual Drawing Primitives
+=============================
+
+affine sx,rx,ry,sy,tx,ty
+arc x0,y0 x1,y1 a0,a1
+bezier x0,y0  ...  xn,yn
+circle originX,originY perimX,perimY
+clip-path url(#%s)  (%s is the name of the clip path)
+clip-rule (evenodd|nonzero)
+clip-units (userSpace|userSpaceOnUse|objectBoundingBox)
+color x,y (point|replace|floodfill|filltoborder|reset)
+decorate (none|underline|overline|line-through)
+ellipse centerX,centerY radiusX,radiusY arcStart,arcEnd
+fill colorspec
+fill-opacity opacity[%]
+fill-rule (evenodd|nonzero)
+font fontname
+font-family familyname (e.g. "helvetica")
+font-size pointsize
+font-stretch (all|normal|ultra-condensed|extra-condensed|condensed|
+              semi-condensed|semi-expanded|expanded|extra-expanded|
+              ultra-expanded)
+font-style (all|normal|italic|oblique)
+font-weight (all|normal|bold|100|200|300|400|500|600|700|800|900)
+gradient-units (userSpace|userSpaceOnUse|objectBoundingBox)
+gravity (NorthWest|North|NorthEast|West|Center|East|SouthWest|
+         South|SouthEast)
+image (Add|Atop|Bumpmap|Clear|CopyBlue|CopyGreen|CopyOpacity|CopyRed|
+       Copy|Difference|In|Minus|Multiply|Out|Over|Plus|Subtract|Xor)
+       dest_x,dest_y dest_width,dest_height 'filename'
+line startX,startY endX,endY
+matte x,y (point|replace|floodfill|filltoborder|reset)
+offset  ???
+opacity value[%]
+path 'SVG-compatible path arguments'
+point x,y
+polygon x1,y1, x2,y2, x3,y3, ..., xN,yN
+polyline x1,y1, x2,y2, x3,y3, ..., xN,yN
+pop clip-path
+pop defs
+pop gradient
+pop graphic-context
+pop pattern
+push clip-path %s  (%s is the name of the clip path)
+push defs
+push gradient id linear x1,y1 x2,y2
+push gradient id radial cx,cy fx,fy r
+push graphic-context
+push pattern id x,y width,height
+rectangle upperLeftX,upperLeftY lowerRightX,lowerRightY
+rotate angle
+roundrectangle upperLeftX,upperLeftY lowerRightX,lowerRightY cornerWidth,cornerHeight
+scale x,y
+skewX angle
+skewY angle
+stop-color colorspec offset
+stroke colorspec
+stroke-antialias truth-value (0 or 1)
+stroke-dasharray (none|comma-delimited-numeric-list)
+stroke-dashoffset dashoffset
+stroke-linecap (butt|round|square)
+stroke-linejoin (butt|miter|round|square)
+stroke-miterlimit limit
+stroke-opacity opacity[%]
+stroke-width linewidth
+text x,y "some text"
+text-antialias (0|1)
+text-undercolor colorspec
+translate x,y
+viewbox x1 y1 x1 y2 (e.g. "viewbox 0 0 640 480")

+// This may look like C code, but it is really -*- C++ -*-

+

+

+

+  // Forward decl
+  class BlobRef;
+
+  class MagickDLLDecl Blob
+  {
+
+  public:
+
+    enum Allocator
+    {
+      MallocAllocator,
+      NewAllocator
+    };
+
+    // Default constructor
+    Blob ( void );
+
+    // Construct object with data, making a copy of the supplied data.
+    Blob ( const void* data_, size_t length_ );
+
+    // Copy constructor (reference counted)
+    Blob ( const Blob& blob_ );
+
+    // Destructor (reference counted)
+    virtual       ~Blob ();
+
+    // Assignment operator (reference counted)
+    Blob&         operator= ( const Blob& blob_ );
+
+    // Update object contents from Base64-encoded string representation.
+    void          base64 ( const std::string base64_ );
+    // Return Base64-encoded string representation.
+    std::string   base64 ( void );
+
+    // Update object contents, making a copy of the supplied data.
+    // Any existing data in the object is deallocated.
+    void          update ( const void* data_, size_t length_ );
+
+    // Update object contents, using supplied pointer directly (no
+    // copy). Any existing data in the object is deallocated.  The user
+    // must ensure that the pointer supplied is not deleted or
+    // otherwise modified after it has been supplied to this method.
+    // Specify allocator_ as "MallocAllocator" if memory is allocated
+    // via the C language malloc() function, or "NewAllocator" if
+    // memory is allocated via C++ 'new'.
+    void          updateNoCopy ( void* data_, size_t length_,
+                                 Allocator allocator_ = NewAllocator );
+
+    // Obtain pointer to data. The user should never try to modify or
+    // free this data since the Blob class manages its own data. The
+    // user must be finished with the data before allowing the Blob to
+    // be destroyed since the pointer is invalid once the Blob is
+    // destroyed.
+    const void*   data ( void ) const;
+
+    // Obtain data length
+    size_t length ( void ) const;
+
+  protected:
+
+  private:
+    BlobRef * _blobRef;
+  };
+
+} // namespace Magick
+
+#endif // Magick_BlobRef_header

title: Potential NULL Pointer Dereference in MagickCore
security_topic: null pointer dereference validity and fix status
qa_summary: Whether the reported null pointer dereference issues in ImageMagick were confirmed and fixed in 7.1.2.15, based on the maintainer’s reproduction and patch announcement.

comments.author: waugustus
waugustus
comments.body:
Thanks for the feedback.

The findings are based on manual, source-level control-flow analysis and review of error-handling paths.

I’m working on a minimal reproducible input and will follow up with an ASan crash trace (or gdb backtrace) if I can confirm reachability.

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body: Thank you for reporting the issue. We have successfully reproduced it and are actively working on a patch to resolve the issue. You can expect this patch to be merged into the [main GIT branch](https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick), later today. As part of our commitment to quality, this fix will also be included in the upcoming [beta releases of ImageMagick](https://imagemagick.org/archive/beta/) by tomorrow. Your patience and feedback are greatly appreciated.

comments.author: ylwango613
comments.body:
Maybe there are two potential NPD, the alpha-as-PNG path around line 12356 and the main JDAT-writing path around line 12732.
In coders/png.c in WriteOneJNGImage(), two ImageToBlob() results were originally used without an immediate NULL check and could cause a null-pointer dereference if ImageToBlob() fails but the code still passes blob to WriteBlob()/crc32().
In contrast, other coders typically add a guard right after ImageToBlob(), for example coders/cals.c around line 570, coders/pdf.c around line 1104, coders/ps3.c around line 311, and coders/magick.c around line 13279.

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body: Thank you for reporting the issue and the suggested patch. We need to hold off on the commit for a few days while we prep a new release.

comments.author: ylwango613
comments.body:
### ImageMagick version

7.1.2-13

### Operating system

Linux

### Operating system, version and so on

22.04.5 64bit

### Description

During FITS parsing, NAXIS1 and NAXIS2 (image width and height) are first multiplied as int values to compute the total number of pixels; when the values are large, this arithmetic overflows and yields an incorrect pixel count. This can cause the program to crash or abort parsing (denial of service), or lead to excessive memory allocation and potential out-of-bounds access.

### Steps to Reproduce

### PoC
use the following fits:
[[fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits)](https://fits.gsfc.nasa.gov/samples/WFPC2u5780205r_c0fx.fits)

Use the follow py file to transfer it to 65536*65537
```
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys
from typing import Tuple, Dict

FITS_BLOCK = 2880
CARD = 80

def _read_cards(buf: bytes, max_cards: int = 4096) -> Tuple[list[bytes], int]:
    """
    Read cards from buf[0:] in 80-byte increments until finding the END card (keyword == 'END').
    Returns (cards, header_len_bytes), where header_len_bytes is the padded header length (2880-aligned).
    """
    cards = []
    end_index = None

    # Need to at least cover up to END; typically primary header won't be too long, setting an upper limit here
    for i in range(0, min(len(buf), max_cards * CARD), CARD):
        card = buf[i:i + CARD]
        if len(card) < CARD:
            break
        cards.append(card)
        keyword = card[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").rstrip()
        if keyword == "END":
            end_index = i + CARD
            break

    if end_index is None:
        raise ValueError("Cannot find END card in the first part of the file (primary header seems corrupted).")

    # Total header length needs to be padded to 2880 boundary (ImageMagick code will read the padding)
    header_len = ((end_index + FITS_BLOCK - 1) // FITS_BLOCK) * FITS_BLOCK
    return cards, header_len

def _parse_key_value(card: bytes) -> Tuple[str, str]:
    """
    Parse the keyword and value string from a card (as lenient as possible).
    """
    kw = card[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").strip()
    rest = card[8:].decode("ascii", errors="replace")
    return kw, rest

def _get_int_value_from_card_rest(rest: str) -> int | None:
    """
    Extract an integer from the card[8:] string (handles '= <num>' format).
    """
    s = rest
    if len(s) == 0:
        return None
    if s[0] != "=":
        return None
    # Skip "= ", then strip
    s = s[1:]
    if s.startswith(" "):
        s = s[1:]
    s = s.strip()
    # Value may have a comment "/ ..."
    if "/" in s:
        s = s.split("/", 1)[0].strip()
    # FITS integers are typically right-aligned and may have a sign
    try:
        return int(s, 10)
    except ValueError:
        return None

def _format_int_card(keyword: str, value: int, comment: str = "") -> bytes:
    """
    Generate a standard FITS 80-byte card: KEYWORD= <value> / comment
    Note: keyword must be <=8 bytes and ASCII.
    """
    kw = (keyword[:8]).ljust(8)
    rhs = f"= {value:20d}"  # Common FITS format: numeric field width 20
    if comment:
        rhs += f" / {comment}"
    rhs = rhs[:72].ljust(72)
    card = (kw + rhs).encode("ascii", errors="strict")
    if len(card) != CARD:
        raise AssertionError("card length is not 80 bytes")
    return card

def _extract_primary_header_fields(cards: list[bytes]) -> Dict[str, int]:
    fields: Dict[str, int] = {}
    for c in cards:
        kw, rest = _parse_key_value(c)
        kw_low = kw.lower()
        if kw_low in ("bitpix", "naxis", "naxis1", "naxis2", "naxis3", "simple"):
            v = _get_int_value_from_card_rest(rest)
            if v is not None:
                fields[kw_low] = v
    return fields

def patch_naxis(in_path: str, out_path: str, new_naxis1: int, new_naxis2: int) -> None:
    data = open(in_path, "rb").read()

    cards, header_len = _read_cards(data)
    fields = _extract_primary_header_fields(cards)

    if "bitpix" not in fields:
        raise ValueError("BITPIX not found in primary header; cannot compute data size safely.")
    if "naxis" not in fields:
        raise ValueError("NAXIS not found in primary header.")
    bitpix = fields["bitpix"]
    naxis = fields["naxis"]

    if naxis < 2:
        # You're now changing NAXIS1/2; if naxis<2, the FITS primary HDU isn't a 2D image
        # ImageMagick code also requires rows/columns > 0 to proceed
        # Here we directly set NAXIS to 2 (conservative approach)
        naxis = 2

    if bitpix == 0 or (abs(bitpix) % 8) != 0:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported BITPIX={bitpix} for this patcher (expect 8/16/32/64/-32/-64).")
    bytes_per_pixel = abs(bitpix) // 8

    if new_naxis1 <= 0 or new_naxis2 <= 0:
        raise ValueError("new NAXIS1/NAXIS2 must be positive.")

    # --- Modify header cards (don't change card count/total bytes, only modify corresponding card content)
    def replace_or_append(keyword: str, value: int):
        nonlocal cards
        key_upper = keyword.upper()
        replaced = False
        for idx, c in enumerate(cards):
            kw = c[0:8].decode("ascii", errors="replace").strip().upper()
            if kw == key_upper:
                cards[idx] = _format_int_card(key_upper, value)
                replaced = True
                break
        if not replaced:
            # Inserting a new card before END: this would change header length and subsequent offsets.
            # To "never break the structure", we don't insert.
            # In actual FITS, NAXIS1/2 should exist; if not, the original file is very atypical.
            raise ValueError(f"{key_upper} card not found; refusing to insert cards (would shift the file).")

    # If needed, first set NAXIS to 2 (prerequisite: NAXIS card originally exists)
    if "naxis" in fields:
        replace_or_append("NAXIS", naxis)
    else:
        raise ValueError("NAXIS card not found; cannot safely patch without shifting.")

    replace_or_append("NAXIS1", new_naxis1)
    replace_or_append("NAXIS2", new_naxis2)

    # --- Reassemble header and maintain its length as the original header_len (2880-aligned)
    new_header = b"".join(cards)
    if len(new_header) > header_len:
        # Theoretically won't happen (we didn't insert cards)
        raise ValueError("Patched header unexpectedly exceeds original padded header length.")
    new_header = new_header.ljust(header_len, b" ")

    # --- Handle primary data unit
    old_data = data[header_len:]
    new_data_bytes = new_naxis1 * new_naxis2 * bytes_per_pixel

    # Conservative: only ensure the primary data area is long enough; don't handle extensions (if the original file has extensions, changing dimensions may cause semantic inconsistency)
    if len(old_data) < new_data_bytes:
        new_data = old_data + (b"\x00" * (new_data_bytes - len(old_data)))
    else:
        new_data = old_data[:new_data_bytes]

    # Extra: pad data to 2880 per FITS convention (not mandatory, but more standard)
    pad = (-len(new_data)) % FITS_BLOCK
    if pad:
        new_data += b"\x00" * pad

    with open(out_path, "wb") as f:
        f.write(new_header)
        f.write(new_data)

def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 5:
        print(f"Usage: {sys.argv[0]} <in.fits> <out.fits> <new_naxis1> <new_naxis2>")
        sys.exit(2)

    in_path, out_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
    n1, n2 = int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4])
    patch_naxis(in_path, out_path, n1, n2)
    print("OK:", out_path)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```
Usage:
```
yuelinwang@XXF-GPU-03:/data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/ImageMagick/test++$ python3 112.py 112.fits 112+.fits 65536 65537
OK: 114.fits
```

Use magick to read file
```
./utilities/magick /data/ylwang/LargeScan/targets/ImageMagick/test++/112+.fits null
coders/fits.c:420:56: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 65536 * 65537 cannot be represented in type 'int'
coders/fits.c:436:54: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 65536 * 65537 cannot be represented in type 'int'
```

title: Insecure File Access Due to External Control of Environment Variables in Magick++
security_topic: path traversal via environment-variable-controlled file paths
qa_summary: Whether the path traversal via SRCDIR/MAGICK_FONT can be mitigated by ImageMagick’s documented security policy that denies file reads outside an allowed directory.

comments.author: weaver4VD
urban-warrior
comments.body:
ImageMagick uses this pattern in its demos and test utilities, but these executables are **not** included in a standard installation. When the code is used independently, developers can harden it by sanitizing any user‑controlled paths before passing them to ImageMagick.

As an additional layer of protection, a user may restrict ImageMagick’s filesystem access by denying all reads except those from explicitly allowed directories. A [security policy](https://imagemagick.org/script/security-policy.php) such as the following can enforce this:

```xml
<policymap>
  <!-- Deny all file reads by default -->
  <policy domain="path" rights="none" pattern="*" />

  <!-- Allow reads ONLY from /opt/ImageMagick/ -->
  <policy domain="path" rights="read" pattern="/opt/ImageMagick/*" />
</policymap>
```

How this policy works

- Global deny rule — Blocks all filesystem reads (pattern="*").
- Allow rule — Re‑enables read access only for files located under /opt/ImageMagick/.

All other paths, including system directories such as /etc/, /home/, /var/, and any relative path traversal attempts like ../../,  are denied.

qa_pairs.answer: ImageMagick uses this pattern only in demos and test utilities, and those executables are not included in a standard installation. If the code is used independently, developers should sanitize user-controlled paths before passing them to ImageMagick. As an additional protection, filesystem access can be restricted with an ImageMagick security policy that denies all reads by default and allows reads only from explicitly allowed directories, e.g. denying `pattern="*"` and allowing read access only under `/opt/ImageMagick/*`.

qa_pairs.question: I am using ImageMagick through JNA in a Java server, calling Genesis at server startup and Terminus at server shutdown. `MagickResizeImage` works until the configured time limit is reached; after that point, any further `MagickResizeImage` calls fail with `time limit exceeded`. rubric.text: States that ImageMagick's time-to-live limit is associated with an individual image rather than being a single global timer for all operations.
rubric.source_quote: ImageMagick's time-to-live is image-based, not global.

rubric.text: Identifies the technical way to adjust the per-image time limit: set or modify the image structure's `ttl` member.
rubric.source_quote: It can be modified directly by setting the image structure member `ttl`.

acceptable_alternatives: Answers may describe this as a per-image TTL, per-image deadline, or per-image time budget, and may refer to modifying the underlying Image or MagickCore structure rather than naming `ttl` exactly if the mechanism is clearly per-image. For timeout behavior, answers should receive credit if they explain that ImageMagick checks the limit at certain processing points, especially pixel-cache/pixel-access points, instead of using a preemptive interrupt or hard wall-clock kill.

qa_pairs.question:

  Thread: 1
  Throttle: 0
  Time: 5 seconds
```

But resizing an image takes about 20 seconds even though it throws `time limit exceeded`:

```

magick: time limit exceeded `7_7 mb.png' @ error/cache.c/GetImagePixelCache/1717.

magick "7_7 mb.png" -resize 100x100 out.png  19.35s user 0.77s system 96% cpu 20.807 total

qa_pairs.answer: There is a delay because ImageMagick does not use a signal to abort the process. It checks whether the time limit has been hit when image pixels are accessed, and when it has, it stops executing the next commands. The maintainers do not communicate release dates because they do not know exactly when a release will happen, though they were preparing a new release.

rubric.text: Explains that the configured time limit is not a hard, signal-driven wall-clock kill of the ImageMagick process, so the command may continue for some time after the limit is exceeded.
rubric.source_quote: There is a delay because we don't use a signal to abort the process.

rubric.text: Identifies the enforcement mechanism as cooperative polling during image pixel access, with execution stopping at subsequent command/check points rather than immediately interrupting the current work.
rubric.source_quote: When the pixels of the image are being access we check if a time limit has been hit and when that happens we stop executing of the next commands.

acceptable_alternatives: Equivalent explanations should count if they state that ImageMagick checks the time limit only at certain internal safe points, such as pixel/cache access, and does not asynchronously kill or signal-abort the operation immediately. It is also acceptable to say the delay is due to cooperative timeout enforcement rather than necessarily being stuck in a delegate.

title: file descriptor leak because without proper release handle
security_topic: file descriptor leak in HEIC image handling
qa_summary: Whether the HEIC/HEIF file-descriptor leak that can exhaust PHP-FPM resources is fixed by reusing the existing heif_context instead of calling heif_image_handle_get_context, as the maintainer says they pushed a patch.

comments.author: jem-sh
dlemstra
comments.body: It looks like that part should not call `heif_image_handle_get_context`, we can re-use the heif_context that was created earlier instead. Thanks for reporting this and I just pushed a patch that fixes this.

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7.1.1-36 on Linux / AWS Linux 2023, I am seeing a file descriptor leak when reading HEIC/HEIF files through PHP Imagick. The file descriptor for `/home/wwwuser/4.heic` remains open after `$im->destroy()`, which eventually leads to “too many files opened” in PHP-FPM mode.

Reproducer:

```php
$im = new \Imagick();
$im->setOption('heic:preserve-orientation', true);
$im->readImage('/home/wwwuser/4.heic');
$im->destroy();
```

This appears to be in `coders/heic.c`, around the call to `heif_image_handle_get_context(image_handle)`. I tested adding a release at the end of the relevant block and the leak went away:

```c
#if LIBHEIF_NUMERIC_VERSION >= HEIC_COMPUTE_NUMERIC_VERSION(1,17,0)
    ...........
    heif_context=heif_image_handle_get_context(image_handle);
    ........... 
    ...........
    heif_context_free(heif_context);  // release the internal handle
#endif
```

Should ImageMagick release this handle or otherwise change how it obtains the HEIF context to avoid the leaked file descriptor?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer said that this code path should not call `heif_image_handle_get_context`; it should re-use the `heif_context` that was created earlier instead. A patch was pushed: https://github.com/Planetart/ImageMagick/commit/5133450c0fd430cbe25e75c81e329d64b60eab3e

rubric.text: Identifies the fix direction: this HEIC read path should not obtain a separate context by calling `heif_image_handle_get_context` from the image handle.
rubric.source_quote: that part should not call `heif_image_handle_get_context`

rubric.text: States that the existing HEIF context created earlier in the read flow should be reused/passed through instead of acquiring another one.
rubric.source_quote: we can re-use the heif_context that was created earlier instead

rubric.text: Applies the reused context to the helper paths that need it, so `ReadHEICImageHandle` and depth-image handling receive the existing `heif_context` and use it for HEIF item transformation queries.
rubric.source_quote:
static MagickBooleanType ReadHEICImageHandle(const ImageInfo *image_info,
  Image *image,struct heif_context *heif_context,
  struct heif_image_handle *image_handle,ExceptionInfo *exception)

acceptable_alternatives: An answer can still be correct if it proposes another technically sound way to avoid leaking the HEIF context, such as keeping the `heif_image_handle_get_context` call but ensuring every acquired context is released on all success and error paths. It should not count as correct if it leaves the extra context acquisition unpaired or suggests only destroying the PHP Imagick object without addressing the HEIC coder context ownership.

title: Provide command-line option to disable delegates; or, identify is extremely slow on video files
security_topic: per-invocation disabling of delegates vs security policy configuration
qa_summary: Whether disabling delegates per command is needed to prevent code injection and untrusted input from triggering external commands, and the answer rests on the documented ImageMagick security policy and the `policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="*"` example.

comments.author: Earnestly
comments.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

When attempting to use `magick -ping "$file" -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:` on video files, such as `video/mp4`, IM will delegate to:

```
video:decode =>          "ffmpeg' -nostdin -loglevel error -i '%s' -an -f rawvideo -y %s '%s"
```

For large, or really even small video files, this process can take an extordinary amount of time and cpu usage.

_(Note that interrupting `magick` with `Ctrl-C` does not kill the `ffmpeg` child so the process remains running, nor does it clean up `/tmp` symlinks.)_


### Describe the solution you'd like

Rather than trying to account for each delegate and their potential onerous behaviours, I would very much like the ability to disable all delegates via the command-line.

I'm aware that this might be possible by either modifying `/etc/ImageMagick-7/delegates.xml` or changing the policy in `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`, but both of these require root permissions and effect global usage of `magick` which would not be my intention.

Ideally `magick` could introduce a `-define` which allows me to disable the use of delegates entirely.

_(PS. I am not personally interested in using delegates and so do not need any kind of per-delegate control.)_

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body:
Add `[0]` to your command-line to speed up video processing:

```
magick -ping "$file[0]" -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:
````

Adding a command-line option could be a security issue.  By the default, ImageMagick polices are controlled by the administrator.  If you perform a non-standard install, ImageMagick can instead consult your local `delegates.xml` and you can disable delegates at will by altering the default configuration.

Please consider nicely what you're suggesting. If someone wants to use `magick` in a script, just one command in many, and the author wants some guarantee that arbitrary inputs are not going to wreak havok, there is currently _no_ way to do it.

Because `magick` has no way to disable delegates, and because delegates are user controlled objects, by dint this means any such script may execute arbitrary code based on carefully constructed inputs, whether it's `magick`'s own filename evaluation strategies or full execution control based on delegate.

I disagree with the reasoning that you should follow a design principle of "only have one way to do one thing" when specifically dealing with program configuration. Here "configuration" means any external file that controls the operation of the program. (Environment variables in contrast are more a form of IPC.) Exposing configuration options via the command-line is quite typical and better enables the principle of least priviledge via refinement. Consider openssh as an example of this. _As an aside, the best tools also provide encoders and decoders for all the custom datatypes it employs, typically for custom string encoding, or the capacity to query configuration data in a programmatic manner without expecting each user to implement ad-hoc parsers._ I have managed to find a reasonably sensible way to disable delegates via a `-define`, which I may provide as a PR soon: ```diff diff --git a/MagickCore/constitute.c b/MagickCore/constitute.c index 03fd3ef97..28fe55829 100644 --- a/MagickCore/constitute.c +++ b/MagickCore/constitute.c @@ -621,6 +621,9 @@ MagickExport Image *ReadImage(const ImageInfo *image_info, const MagickInfo *magick_info; + const char + *option; + DecodeImageHandler *decoder; @@ -722,7 +725,9 @@ MagickExport Image *ReadImage(const ImageInfo *image_info, decoder=GetImageDecoder(magick_info); } } - if (decoder != (DecodeImageHandler *) NULL) + option=GetImageOption(image_info,"delegates"); + if (decoder != (DecodeImageHandler *) NULL && + (IsStringTrue(option) != MagickFalse)) { /* Call appropriate image reader based on image type. diff --git a/www/defines.html b/www/defines.html index 6096710df..ceec81be4 100644 --- a/www/defines.html +++ b/www/defines.html @@ -418,6 +418,11 @@ use:

By default, an output filename can contain embedded formatting characters. Use this option to bypass interpreting embedded formatting characters and instead use the filename literally. + + delegates=true + By default allow delegates to execute according to policy. See Security. + + filter:option=value Set a filter option for use with -resize. ```

comments.body:
> > Can you explain why you cannot use [0] ...
> > Because the inputs are user controlled.
> 
> **This is not a very clear and understandable reason, at least for me. Please show some code so that we can understand your issue and why you cannot specify an image name.**

Oh sorry, I'll try to explain my reasoning:

_For a bit of background here is a good article that covers code injection: https://www.more-magic.net/posts/structurally-fixing-injection-bugs.html_

Everything is about encoding. And a lot of it is often accidental: here accidental means that formats are used but not enforced or checked.

Consider a UNIX filename consisting of an arbitrary sequence of bytes, excluding `/`, terminated by a NUL byte. In contrast a Windows filename excludes many more characters and encodes them using the USC-2, it also imparts special meanings to files with specific names.

One consequence of this is that valid UNIX and Windows filenames **cannot be represented** in JSON (as it only supports UTF-8), for example. Yet people do this anyway, largely successfully (this is the accidental part).

When ImageMagick parses filenames and evaluates their meaning, it has implicitly (or explicitly) created a new "encoding" for filenames, which are at variance with UNIX/Windows filenames (like JSON, but different).

The problem arises when the inputs to your program, which you have no control over, uses one encoding (datatype) while the software expects another. There are generally three ways to solve this problem; one is to encode the input to the encoding the program expects, another is to ensure the software treats the input as an array of bytes and to not interpret the bytes at all. The second approach is the ideal solution as it obviates the need to "escape" or "sanitise" inputs.

In other words, by never exposing user-supplied data to code evaluation, you will never suffer from code injection. However, if you cannot do that (such as interpreting image data) then you must enforce the encoding (this is what your oss-fuzz tests are doing) and ensure your parser can deal with malformed input. (cf. Weird Machines)

What I am essentially asking for is a way to provide this data, un-interpreted. Consider SQL and prepared statements as analogous to my request. However if "prepared statements" are not possible (i.e. `filename:literal=true` for both input and output filenames) then I must resort to something like `safe_escape_string_for_real_this_time()`.

If there is no "encoding" for imagemagick filenames, e.g. `png\:\-` as a filename vs. `png:-` as special meaning to imagemagick, then I can only detect this encoding/datatype, check it, and error out as a "type mismatch". This is the third option.

_PS. A good set of examples are shell scripts which rely on word splitting that only work when file names don't contain spaces, see the myriad ways shell scripts tend to accidently practice code injection without realising: https://mywiki.wooledge.org/BashProgramming/05_

Sorry if a bit long winded, but hopefully it makes my point of view a bit clearer.

_PPS. Yes, this started as an issue with `ffmpeg` being slow when attempting to query file information, but once I saw `magick -list delegates` I decided that I would much rather completely disable this feature for my scripts which don't need it._

comments.author: urban-warrior
comments.body:
The administrator has full control over the machine, allowing them to decide how ImageMagick should operate in their environment. This approach is commonly adopted on both Linux and Windows hosts. Alternatively, the administrator may choose to install ImageMagick using the "no-install" option. By doing so, they delegate the responsibility for configuration to the user.

In such cases, the user gains the flexibility to override the system's delegate, security policies, and other settings by creating a custom configuration within their home directory. qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7, I am using `magick -ping "$file" -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:` on user-controlled inputs. For video files such as `video/mp4`, ImageMagick delegates to ffmpeg:

```
video:decode =>          "ffmpeg' -nostdin -loglevel error -i '%s' -an -f rawvideo -y %s '%s"
```

This can take an extraordinary amount of time and CPU, and interrupting `magick` with Ctrl-C does not kill the `ffmpeg` child or clean up `/tmp` symlinks. I also found that because delegates are commands resolved via `PATH`, a crafted environment/input can execute arbitrary code, for example:

```sh
$ cat ffmpeg
#!/bin/sh --
echo hi > owned

$ PATH=.:$PATH magick -ping video/1917.mp4 -format '%[mime:type]\n' info:
magick: insufficient image data in file `/tmp/magick-5EIzi9um6SIwIOvJRf1zJ0nd4fuEaiaD' @ error/webp.c/ReadWEBPImage/560.

$ cat owned
hi
```

I want a per-invocation way for a script to avoid delegate execution, rather than editing global `/etc/ImageMagick-7/delegates.xml` or `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`. If a distribution disables execution of delegates by default, how can a user enable delegates for one specific requirement? Is it all-or-nothing based on distribution/admin policy?
qa_pairs.answer: The security policy can allow all delegates, some delegates, or none. If the administrator disables some or all delegates, a user cannot enable them without administrative privileges; that is the administrator’s role in dictating policy for the environment. If the administrator wants to delegate policy decisions to users, they can install ImageMagick with the `disable-install` option.

rubric.text: States that delegate execution is controlled by ImageMagick security policy, which can allow all delegates, selected delegates, or no delegates.
rubric.source_quote: The security policy allows all delegates, some, or none.

rubric.text: States that if an administrator disables some or all delegates, an ordinary user cannot re-enable them without administrative privileges.
rubric.source_quote: If the administrator disables some or all the delegates, the user cannot enable them without administrative privileges

rubric.text: Explains that administrator-controlled policy is intentional: the administrator dictates ImageMagick policy for the environment.
rubric.source_quote: that is the role of the administrator, to dictate policy over their environment

rubric.text: Mentions the supported way for an administrator to let users control policy decisions: install ImageMagick with the `disable-install` option.
rubric.source_quote: if the administrator wants to delegate policy decisions to the user, they can install ImageMagick with the `disable-install` option

acceptable_alternatives: Answers may phrase the result as: delegate use is governed by policy.xml/security policy rather than a per-invocation CLI flag; a non-admin cannot override a restrictive administrator or distribution policy; user-controlled delegate policy is only possible if the administrator installs/configures ImageMagick to allow user policy control, such as with the `disable-install` option.

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7.1.1-43 on Windows 10, some EXR files cause `magick` to crash when decoded. This appears to be due to the underlying OpenEXR library coming up with no channels, while `coders/exr.c` assumes at least one channel in `InitializeEXRChannels` when checking the channel name prefix.

Reproduction:

`magick Kapaa.exr out.jpg`

qa_pairs.answer: Patch link: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/commit/e11a59d28561d9e648705d8b55f68f085223008e

rubric.text: Stops processing a tiled EXR as soon as an unsupported tile-level configuration is detected, returning failure instead of continuing into later decode/channel logic that can crash.

acceptable_alternatives: Any sound fix that validates/rejects unsupported EXR tiled level counts before continuing is acceptable, including returning an error status, jumping to existing cleanup-and-fail handling, or otherwise aborting the read path after raising the unsupported-levels error. It does not need to use the exact return statement shown, as long as it prevents subsequent channel initialization/pixel processing on the unsupported EXR.

title: Converting some images to PICT results in files that will crash a classic Mac system
security_topic: PICT file format validity causing classic Mac OS crash
qa_summary: Whether ImageMagick’s PICT encoder is producing malformed files that crash classic Mac OS, and the answer rests on the cited Inside Macintosh: Volume V documentation plus the specific ImageMagick source lines in pict.c that should compare `bytes_per_line > 250`.

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body:
### ImageMagick version

7.1.1-34

### Operating system

MacOS

### Operating system, version and so on

macOS 13.6.5

### Description

Converting certain images to a PICT file will produce files that will crash the system when attempting to view them on a classic Mac OS system. I've reproduced the crash on Macintosh System 7.1, Mac OS 8, and Mac OS 9.

Converting the PICT file back to a png using ImageMagick does not present any issues. I have not yet identified a modern app that presents a problem viewing the bad PICT file ImageMagick produces.

I've attached both the png file that exhibits this bug and the resulting PICT file that will crash a classic Mac.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Convert the attached png file to a pict with the following:
    `magick bad.png bad.pict`
2. Copy `bad.pict` to a system running classic Mac OS and open it in any application that can view PICT files (such as SimpleText)
3. System freezes or displays a system error

### Images

![bad](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b782b586-90d3-40fc-bde1-8438975e597d)
[bad.pict.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18142059/bad.pict.zip)

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body:
> Perhaps Apple changed the PICT format between old classic Mac and newer OSX versions.

I don't believe that's the case. The latest PICT format is "Extended Version 2" which has been around since at least the 1990s, and which is what ImageMagick is producing based off of the version information in the outputted file.

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body:
SimpleText uses the same system-level API to display a PICT as every other app in classic Mac OS. I can trigger the crash using any application that can read PICT files.

It's possible that their implementation has a bug that would cause it to crash reading an otherwise valid PICT, but I think that's unlikely. Also, given that Apple's PICT implementation from classic Mac OS is essentially the canonical implementation, I think we need to assume that ImageMagick is producing invalid files.

comments.author: briankendall
comments.body: I do believe I found the issue. The key is in page 119 of Inside Macintosh: Volume V, where it describes how the pixel data of a PICT should be written out. Here's a screen shot of the relevant section: The key part is where it says "If rowBytes > 250". In `bad.pict`, rowBytes is 240, but the `byteCount` of each scanline is two bytes rather than one. I just manually modified the file so that the `byteCount` entries for each scanline is only one byte, and it fixed the file, in that classic Mac OS can now properly read it. (See : [fixed.pict.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18159393/fixed.pict.zip) ) This bug apparently affects ImageMagick's PICT reader as well, as it's unable to open `fixed.pict` and produces this error: error/pict.c/ReadPICTImage/1267. In fact, I think that points me to the error, see: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/blob/b77eb776838b6039834948bb63f8106a7980554b/coders/pict.c#L504 That should be: if (bytes_per_line > 250) Same here: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/blob/b77eb776838b6039834948bb63f8106a7980554b/coders/pict.c#L694 And here too: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/blob/b77eb776838b6039834948bb63f8106a7980554b/coders/pict.c#L1087

comments.author: bobfriesenhahn
comments.body: Failing to be able to read the existing PICT files that ImageMagick wrote for perhaps 30 years seems pretty brutal.

qa_pairs.question:
In ImageMagick 7.1.1-34 on macOS 13.6.5, converting certain PNG images to PICT produces a file that freezes or shows a system error when opened on classic Mac OS systems. I reproduced this on Macintosh System 7.1, Mac OS 8, and Mac OS 9, using any application that can view PICT files such as SimpleText. Converting the PICT back to PNG using ImageMagick works, and I have not identified a modern app that has trouble viewing the bad PICT. Reproduction:

1. Convert the attached PNG to PICT:
   `magick bad.png bad.pict`
2. Copy `bad.pict` to a system running classic Mac OS and open it in a PICT-viewing application such as SimpleText.
3. The system freezes or displays a system error.

![bad](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/b782b586-90d3-40fc-bde1-8438975e597d)
[bad.pict.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18142059/bad.pict.zip)

The PNG was attached as `bad.png`, and the crashing output was attached as `bad.pict.zip`. The PICT appears to be Extended Version 2, not a newer macOS-only format. What is wrong with ImageMagick’s generated PICT file, and what in the PICT reader/writer should be changed?
qa_pairs.answer: The issue was identified from Inside Macintosh: Volume V: when PICT pixel data is written, the scanline byteCount is one byte unless `rowBytes > 250`. In `bad.pict`, `rowBytes` is 240, but ImageMagick wrote each scanline `byteCount` as two bytes; manually changing those entries to one byte made classic Mac OS read the file. The same condition affects ImageMagick’s PICT reader, which could not open the fixed file and reported `error/pict.c/ReadPICTImage/1267.`; the checks in `coders/pict.c` at lines 504, 694, and 1087 should use `if (bytes_per_line > 250)`. PR: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/pull/7840/

rubric.text: Correctly identifies the file-format rule and root cause: PICT scanline byteCount is one byte unless rowBytes is greater than 250, and ImageMagick was writing a two-byte byteCount for a rowBytes value such as 240.
rubric.source_quote: The key part is where it says "If rowBytes > 250". In `bad.pict`, rowBytes is 240, but the `byteCount` of each scanline is two bytes rather than one.

rubric.text: Correctly concludes that the generated PICT is invalid because of ImageMagick’s encoding, not merely a classic Mac OS viewer quirk.
rubric.source_quote: I just manually modified the file so that the `byteCount` entries for each scanline is only one byte, and it fixed the file, in that classic Mac OS can now properly read it.

rubric.text: Proposes the essential writer-side fix: choose a two-byte packed scanline length only when bytes_per_line/rowBytes is greater than 250, otherwise write a one-byte length.
rubric.source_quote: if (bytes_per_line > 250)

rubric.text: Recognizes that the PICT reader must use the same >250 threshold when deciding whether to read a one-byte or two-byte scanline length, so it can read conforming files with rowBytes <= 250.
rubric.source_quote: This bug apparently affects ImageMagick's PICT reader as well, as it's unable to open `fixed.pict`

acceptable_alternatives: Equivalent fixes should count if they implement the PICT rule by any sound means, such as centralizing the byteCount-size decision or comparing rowBytes/bytes_per_line against 250 in helper code. Answers need not name the exact source lines, PR, commit, or version. Do not require the literal condition spelling as long as the behavior is two-byte counts only for values greater than 250 and one-byte counts for 250 or below. An answer that changes only the writer but not the reader is incomplete for this question; an answer using the old >200 threshold or using >=250 is incorrect.

title: MNG file consumes all RAM

comments.author: dlemstra
comments.body: You should add `<policy domain="resource" name="list-length" value=""/>` to your policy.xml file and set the value to the maximum number of images that you want. Your input file contains a ridiculous `LOOP` value and that is why it's trying to create `2147483647` images.

qa_pairs.question: In ImageMagick 7.1.1-38 Q16-HDRI x86_64 22398 on Gentoo Linux, running `magick identify _7AD4C6FDA1664599A5DE1A7FF89000C2` on the attached MNG file `_7AD4C6FDA1664599A5DE1A7FF89000C2` causes `magick` to consume all system RAM until it crashes. qa_pairs.answer: Add `<policy domain="resource" name="list-length" value=""/>` to `policy.xml` and set the value to the maximum number of images you want to allow. The input file contains a ridiculous `LOOP` value, causing ImageMagick to try to create `2147483647` images.

rubric.text: Specifies the mitigation as setting ImageMagick's `resource` policy `list-length` in `policy.xml` to cap the maximum number of images that may be created or processed.
rubric.source_quote: Add `<policy domain="resource" name="list-length" value=""/>` to `policy.xml` and set the value to the maximum number of images you want to allow.

rubric.text: Explains the cause as the MNG input having an excessive `LOOP` value that makes ImageMagick attempt to create 2,147,483,647 images.
rubric.source_quote: The input file contains a ridiculous `LOOP` value, causing ImageMagick to try to create `2147483647` images.

acceptable_alternatives: It is acceptable to give the same mitigation with an explicit nonempty numeric `value` for `list-length`, or to describe it as limiting ImageMagick's image-list length/resource policy rather than quoting the exact XML. It is also acceptable to describe the root cause as an enormous MNG animation loop/frame count causing billions of images to be instantiated, even if the exact number 2147483647 is omitted.
